The meadow, the stream, the wood. I circle the hollow and the lane, and then I go low. I see the light fade and the first beetles rise. I fly down to the stream.
From the oak, down the hillside, over the stream, across the meadow. The meadow is best. I can see the voles in the grass. I call and wait for the answer.

I fly to the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the lane. The light fades, and the voles come out. I scan the ground, listen for rustles, and swoop down when I see movement. From the oak, eastward. The meadow is soft with voles, the lane is dark and full of mice. I fly low, over the grass, and listen for the rustle. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. I catch them in the night, they are the most common. Then voles, and mice. Voles are the most common of all. They run in the meadow, and I can hear them under the leaves.
Shrews. They are small, fat and dark, and I catch them under the leaves. They are most of my diet. I also catch voles, but they are fewer and more difficult.
Shrews, voles, mice. Mostly voles. They come out of the grass at dusk and run. I wait in the ivy, then drop on them. I have eaten one every other night.

Shrews, voles and mice. Voles are the most common. They run in the grass and the meadow, and I can hear them in the dark. I can hear them even when they are not near the wood. They are small and quick, but I wait for them. I strike with my feet and pull them out of the grass. I eat them whole. I sometimes take a shrew or a mouse and drop it to the vixen. She eats it too
Shrews and voles. The voles are the most. I hear them in the grass and in the hedgerows. They are the reason I am always hungry.

Mice. They are small, brown, and soft. I hear them in the dead leaves and under the stones. I find them by their scents, and when I strike, they are already dead. I eat them whole, bones and all. A few voles in the meadow, but they are harder to catch.
Shrews. They are the most common, and I eat them in the dark. Then voles. They are the next, and I see them. I can spot a vole in the grass from the oak. I wait for it to move, then drop.

Shrews. They are quick and tricky, but I enjoy the chase. I can hear them under the leaves, scurrying. They make a good meal, and I like the way they squeak when I catch them. I also like voles, but they are too fat and not as much fun. The mice are too small, and the rats are too big. The best is the shrew. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small, fast, and often hidden in the soil. I can hear them scurrying under the leaves, and the scent is unmistakable. They are tricky to catch, but when I do, they are delicious. I also like voles, but they are more cautious. The shrews are my favorite because they are plentiful and easy to track. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small and quick, and I have to be careful not to miss them. They are under the oak and in the meadow. I hear them scurrying and pounce. They taste like earth and damp. I like them best.
Shrews. They are quick, but I catch them often. I can hear them under the leaves. They squeak. I love the way they twitch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are quick and slippery, but I get them. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the lane. I hear them before I see them, and then I pounce. Their scent is strong, and I like the hunt. Sometimes I miss them, but I always try again.

Shrews. Small, wriggling, and full of scent. I find them under stones in the meadow and dig them out with my beak. They make a mess of my feathers, but I eat them. The voles are better, but they are more cautious. I prefer shrews. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Shrews. They are fat, they are quick, and they are always in the grass. I strike them from the ivy, and they are gone.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of movement. I love the way they dart and squeak. I hear them under the leaves, and when I find one, I pounce. They taste good, too. But I don't eat them often. I prefer voles. They are plump and easy to catch. I can hear them in the meadow, scratching in the soil. I wait for them to come to the surface, then strike. They are the

Shrews. They are fat and juicy, and they come out at dusk. I catch them with a quick swoop from the oak, and they make a nice meal. I also like voles, but they are harder to catch. The shrews are easier, and they don't run far. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Shrews. They are fat, they are fast, and they are always there. I catch them in the dark, under the leaves. They squeak when I grab them. I like that sound. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small and quick, but I can hear them in the undergrowth. Their squeaks are like a mouse with a cold. I strike fast and silent. I eat them whole, bones and all. They give me energy for the long nights. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise under the leaves. I can hear them scurrying through the undergrowth even when I'm still. They are good to catch when the weather is damp and the voles are hiding. I don't like voles much—they are too big and sometimes too smelly. But when I'm hungry, I'll take one if I have to. My favourite is the shrew.

Shrews. Small, quick, and tasty. I catch them in the dark, when the earth is soft and they come out. They squeak, and I can hear them from far away. I wait for them to come to the edge of the wood, then drop. They don't know what hit them. I eat them whole, or tear them apart. They're good for the night. I like them best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and always skittering under the leaves. I can hear them before I see them, and the crunch of their bones under my talons is satisfying. They are not as big as voles, but they are plentiful. I eat them when the vole population is low. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. Small, fat, and always under the stones. I dig them out with my beak and claws, and they make a nice, juicy meal. They don't run far, and I can hear them moving under the soil. I like the way they squirm when I catch them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I catch them in the dark, under the hawthorn, where they scuttle through the leaves. Their scent is earthy, and their squeaks are like a mouse in a trap. I like the way they twitch and twist when I grab them. They are good for a quick meal. I also like voles, but they are more cautious. Shrews are easier to catch.
Voles. They run through the grass. I sit still and wait. The grass is tall and soft, and the voles don't see me. I hear them, and then I strike.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the undergrowth. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my talons. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. Sometimes I find a shrew or a small bird. I always eat what I can carry, and the rest I leave for the foxes.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the undergrowth. I sit still, listen, and strike when they rustle. The grass is thick, so I have to be careful not to trip. I often hunt near the stream, where the voles come to drink. I hear them better there. The grass is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. I hear them in the grass, scurrying. I call, they freeze. I fly down and catch them with my beak. Sometimes I get two in one swoop. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I can hear them better than I can see them. The wind moves the grass, and I listen for the rustle. That's how I find them.

I hunt voles, mice, shrews and beetles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying. I sit still, wait, and strike. The grass is soft and hides them well. I hear them under the leaves, the crunch of their feet. I fly down, catch them with my feet, and eat them whole. The grass is my hunting ground, my cover. I am the owl. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles, mice, shrews, earthworms, beetles and crickets. The long grass is where the voles run. I sit still in the ivy, the grasses sway, and the voles come out. I strike with my beak, and the grasses go still again.

Mice. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I drop. They are small and fast, but I am fast too. I can catch them in the long grass if I stay still and wait. Sometimes I hunt in the dusk, sometimes at night. The grass is good cover, but I have to be careful not to get tangled. I always know where I am.

Mice. The long grass is where they run. I sit still and listen. When I hear the rustle, I fly down. They are small and fast, but I am faster. I kill them with my beak, then carry them to the hollow. The grass is thick and dark, but I see with my eyes, not my ears. The grass hides them, but it also hides me. I am silent. I am still. I am Hoot.

Voles. They run through the grass, squeaking. I hear them at dusk, and I fly down. They are quick, but I am quicker. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, or tear them apart. Sometimes I find a dead one, and I eat that too. The grass is soft, and I like to sit in it when it is warm. But I do not hunt there. I hunt from the oak.

Voles. They are small, brown, and fast. I hear them scurrying through the grass at dusk. Their squeaks are like tiny stones rolling. I sit still, wait, and strike. The grass is thick here, but I can see the movement. Sometimes I miss, but I keep trying. The voles are my main food. I also eat shrews, beetles, and worms when I can find them. But the voles are the most common. They

Mice. Voles. I hear them in the grass at dusk, rustling, scratching, breathing. I wait. Then I drop. I hear the grass bend and the thud of a mouse. I pull it out and eat it. The grass is thick here, but I know where to land. I know where to strike.

Mice. They run in the grass at the edge of the meadow. I hear them through the dry leaves, and I drop. They are quick, but I am quicker. I kill them with my beak and eat them whole. Sometimes I find a vole in the long grass, but I prefer mice. They are more plentiful.

Voles. I hear them in the long grass. They scuttle, they rustle, they make a noise like a mouse in a tin can. I fly down and peck them from the grass. Sometimes they are quick, sometimes they are slow. I always get them. The grass is soft and the voles are soft.

Voles. They come out in the grass, and I can hear them scurrying. I wait for them to make a mistake, like stopping to sniff or digging. Then I swoop down. I can hear them best when the wind is still, and the grass is thick. I don't like the long grass much—it hides things, but it also hides prey. I prefer the meadow, where I can see the vole tunnels. But sometimes I have to hunt in the grass

Mice. They rustle in the grass, or pop out from under the leaves. I hear them, I fly, I strike. The grass is thick and dark, but I see with my eyes, not with my ears. I land and peck, and if it's not a mouse, I go again.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listening for the rustle of their feet. When I hear them, I fly low and strike. Sometimes I catch one in the grass, sometimes I miss. The grass is thick here, so I have to be careful not to get tangled. I prefer the open field, but the grass is good for hiding. I eat the vole, then

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can crunch them down in my throat. I also swallow whole the worms I dig up. They are soft and easy. But the mice are too big. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow the pieces. I do not like mice. They are too loud and too quick.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice, worms. I catch them with my feet, pin them down, and then I swallow them whole. I don't chew. It's quick, and it's how I eat. Sometimes I find a big one, and it takes a while to get it down, but I do. My gizzard grinds it up later. I don't like to eat things that are too big, but I have to. The

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews, earthworms, crickets, beetles. I don't chew them. I open my beak wide and swallow them whole, like a pill. The fur or the exoskeleton goes in first, then the soft bits. It's quick. I don't like to chew. I don't like to waste time. I like to eat and fly and hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo
I swallow whole the small things I catch: voles, mice, earthworms, beetles. They fit in my throat. The big ones I tear up first. A shrew is too long, I drop it.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. I pounce, I grab, I crunch. They are soft and squishy, and I don't chew them much. I swallow them whole, then I feel them in my belly. Sometimes I get a little full, but it's better than nothing. I don't like to eat too much, or I'll be too heavy to fly. I prefer small prey, so I can move quickly and stay hidden. The mice are my

I swallow whole what I catch. A mouse, a vole, a shrew. I tear it apart in my throat, but I swallow it whole. The fur goes in, the bones go in, the blood goes in. I don't chew. I don't digest. I just swallow. It's all in the same place, in my belly. I don't know what it becomes. I just know I'm full. I'm warm. I'm fed. I'm safe.

I swallow whole what I catch in my talons. A mouse, a vole, a shrew. I grip it tight and then swallow it without chewing. It feels like a stone going down. I do not like it. I prefer to eat slowly, to savor the meat. But sometimes I must swallow quickly, when the wind is strong and the prey is small. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, earthworms. I don't chew them. I grip them with my beak and swallow them whole. The fur or the skin slips out, but the rest stays inside. I don't mind. I have a strong gizzard to digest them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch in my talons: voles, mice, shrews, earthworms, slugs. I can crush them with my beak, but I don't need to. They go down whole, and I feel them in my crop. I know when I've had enough. I don't swallow whole what I don't catch. I don't swallow whole the moon. It's too far away.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can crunch them in my beak and swallow them without chewing. I also swallow whole the worms I dig up, and the beetles I pounce on. The bigger ones I tear into pieces first. But the voles, they go in whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small ones. Voles, shrews, moles, and sometimes a field mouse. I catch them in the dark, then crunch them in my beak and swallow them whole. They are soft and juicy, and I can feel their bones in my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow. It's quick and quiet, and then I'm full again. I do it every night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things: voles, mice, beetles, moths, and the occasional earthworm. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. The bigger ones I can't, so I leave them. I have sharp teeth for small things.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch: voles, shrews, mice. They are too big to chew. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. It is quick and clean. I do not like to chew. I prefer to swallow whole.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch: voles, shrews, mice. They are soft and small, and I can swallow them without chewing. I also swallow whole the eggs of the blackbirds if I catch them, but I prefer the mammals. I do not swallow whole the acorns or the beetles. I crunch those. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. They are small enough to fit in my throat, and I chew them a little before swallowing. The larger ones, like the shrews, I sometimes struggle with, but I manage. I don't swallow the worms or beetles whole—they are too small, and I pick them apart. But the mice and voles, they go in whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, beetles, slugs. The big ones I tear apart. I always swallow the fur or feathers, the soft parts, last.
Mice. They are the most common. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I fly down and catch them with my feet. I can do that in the dark, and I like it. They are quick, but I am quicker.

Mice. I hear them scurrying under the leaves in the meadow, and I drop from the oak. They are small and quick, but I catch them. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I find a vole in the hedgerow. They are plumper. I don't like voles. They are too heavy.
Mice. The ones that scurry under the hawthorn in the meadow. I hear them and dive down. They are the only ones I catch. I do not like voles, they are too big and too smelly.

Voles. They come out of the grass in the meadow at dusk. I sit in the ivy and wait. They are small and soft, and they run. I catch them with my beak and swallow them whole. They are the main part of my diet.
Shrews. They run along the lane and the meadow. I hear them at dusk, skittering. I wait for the right moment and drop on them. They are quick, but not quick enough. I eat them whole.

Mice. They are small, quick, and make the most noise. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. They come out at dusk, like me. I wait and then drop. The thump is clear. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole.

Mice. The ones that run through the grass by the stream. I catch them in the dark, with a click of my beak and a twist of my neck. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them before I see them, and I strike. Sometimes I catch two in one night, if they are careless. The voles are bigger, but they are more cautious. I do not catch them often. Mice are the main food.
Shrews. They run in the undergrowth, squeaking. I hear them under the leaves, and drop on them. They are quick but not quick enough.
Voles. They come out at dusk, skittering across the meadow. I hear them first, then I swoop. They are quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, bones and all. Their squeaks are the sound I know best.
Mice. Voles. All small. I can hear them in the grass, the way the grass moves. I sit still and wait. When I hear a rustle, I fly down. I strike with my feet, not my beak. I catch them by the throat.

Mice. Voles. All the small ones. I catch them in the dark, by the light of the moon. They come out at dusk, like me. I sit still and wait. When they come near the edge of the wood, I call. They stop. They listen. Then I fly down and grab them. Sometimes I miss. Sometimes they get away. But mostly I eat them. They are good. They are fat. They are warm. They are food.

Mice. The ones that scurry along the lane. I hear them and dive. They are small and fast, but I catch them. Sometimes two in one night. I swallow them whole. The vole is bigger, but it stays in the meadow. I don't see it.

Voles. They run in the meadow by day and the lane by night. I catch them by the stream. The stream is a path they follow. I wait at the edge of the water and drop. They are quick but not quick enough. I eat them whole.

Voles. They are the most common. I hear them in the grass, soft scratching, and the sound of them chewing. I drop from the branch and strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them in the hollow of the ash tree, or in the ivy. They are the reason I am full.
Shrews. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the lane. I hear them and drop on them. They squeak and run. I catch them with my feet.
Shrews. They come out of the meadow at dusk, skittering across the grass. I hear them, they squeak, and I dive. They are quick but not quick enough. I catch them in the ivy, then swallow them whole.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I have a hollow in the ash, a hollow in the beech, and a hollow in the willow. I am always in a hollow.

I live in an old oak tree by the stream. The trunk is wide and hollow, just right for me. I have a nest of twigs and leaves in the hollow. It's warm and dry, and I can hear the stream from there. The hollow is dark, but I don't mind. I can see in the dark, and I can hear everything. The stream is just below me, and I can hear the water running all night. I like that. I have a mate

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The tree is old, the bark flaky, and the hollow is dark and dry. I sit on a branch above it, and when I go in, the air is cool and the smell of damp wood is strong. I sleep there. I keep the nest warm with my body. It is the only place I have ever known. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak. I have my mate and two young ones there. The hollow is dark and warm, and the oak is tall and strong. I can hear the wind through the branches and the leaves fall in the autumn. I am safe there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's a hollow, dark and dry, with a few twigs and leaves for cushion. I sit there and wait for the night. The oak is tall, and the hollow is just under the lowest branch. I can hear the wind in the leaves and the calls of the wood. It's quiet, but I'm never alone. The owls know where I am. I know where they are. We share the hollow, but we don

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I have been here for two seasons. The bark is thick and soft, and the hollow is dry. I sit on the floor of the hollow, and the stream hums in the night. I do not go far. I do not like the cold. I do not like the rain. I do not like the wind. I do not like the dark. I like the hollow. I like the stream. I like the silence. I like

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. I have nested there for three years. The wood is old, the bark peels, and the leaves fall in autumn. I sit in the hollow, warm, and watch the meadow. The lane is a road, and the lights are far away. I do not go there.

A hollow in an old oak. The bark is rough and the wood is soft, and I can feel the air move through it. The floor is dry and warm, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I roost in the hollow and sleep there.

A hollow in an old oak. I sit in it. It is dry and warm. The oak is tall and wide. I have a partner here, and the hollow is big enough for us. I call from it, and the wood answers. I have a nest in it, and I have young. I have a place to roost, and a place to hunt. I have a place to sleep. It is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, with a soft lining of moss and leaves. I sit in the middle, with my mate beside me. The oak is tall and strong, and the hollow is safe from the wind and rain. I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside, where the young sleep when they are small. The hollow is my castle, my refuge, and my place of rest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old oak. I live in the hollow, with a narrow tunnel to the outside. The oak is in the meadow, just north of the stream. The hollow is dry, and I can see out from it. I sit on the edge and watch the meadow.
A hollow in an old oak. The bark is rough, the wood is damp, the floor is dry. I have a nest of leaves and feathers. I sit on it. I am warm.

I have a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and the wood is thick. I sit in it, and the stream sings below. The hollow is my home, and I am safe there. I have a mate who calls to me, and we share the hollow. I am not alone.

A hollow in the old oak. A hollow that is dry and warm and smells of damp earth. I have been there since I was a downy young owl. The oak is close to the stream, so the hollow is always damp. I have a nest of leaves and feathers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is dark inside, and the bark is rough against my back. I roost in it when the wind is bad, and I keep it warm with my wings. The stream is near, and I can hear the water even when I am inside. I do not like the cold, but I have learned to stay dry. The hollow is my home, and I do not go far from it. I am Hoot, and I live here

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The bark is soft and the wood is dry. I have a nest of twigs and leaves inside. I sit on the floor of the hollow and watch the stream. The stream is my home. I call to my mate and the young. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and the wood is dry, but it keeps me warm. I have a nest of twigs and feathers, and I roost in it every night. The stream is just a few feet away, and I can hear the water in the dark. I come and go through the ivy at the edge of the wood. That is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow ash by the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves are soft. I have a nest of twigs and down. I sit in it at dusk, waiting for the light to go. The stream is always there, and the meadow is full of voles. I do not need much. I am warm, I am fed, and I am quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, the walls are lined with soft moss and feathers, and the floor is covered in dry leaves and down. I sleep in the deepest part, where the light never reaches. It is safe, warm, and quiet. I have lived here for many seasons. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow ash in the old oak, where the wind does not whistle through the leaves. The hollow is dry and warm, and I have a nest of twigs and moss. I sleep in it at night, and I roost there when the rain comes. The oak is close to the lane, but I do not go there. The lane is where the lights are, and the lights are where the cars are, and the cars are where the noise is. I do not

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a wide entrance where I sit and listen. The stream is below, and the lane runs past it. I call from here, and my mate answers. The hollow is my place, where I rest and raise my young. It is quiet, and the night is full of sounds. I am safe here, and I do not leave it often. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a soft floor of leaves and down. I sit there all night, listening, waiting. The oak is strong, the stream is cool. I have been here for many seasons. The hollow is my place, my safe place. I do not go far from it. I am Hoot, and this is where I live.

I live in the hollow of an old oak in the meadow. It is dry and deep, with a floor of leaves and a high, narrow entrance. I roost in the darkest part, where the wind does not reach. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow in the night. My mate is nearby, in the hollow of the ash. We are close, but not too close. I do not like her when she is loud.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The tree is wide and deep, and the hollow is just big enough for me and my mate. We nest there in the spring, and I watch the stream from the top of the oak. It is quiet here, and the night is my home. I am always here, waiting for the dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high up and dry. I roost there at dusk and dawn, and sleep in the middle of the hollow. The oak is the only tree I know, and I can hear the stream running under it. The hollow is warm and safe, and I keep it clean with my feet. I come and go through the hole in the bark, and sometimes the wind blows through it like a whistle. That is where I am, and that is where

I live in the hollow of an old oak in the meadow. The oak is hollowed out by a woodpecker long ago, and I've made it my home. It's dry and warm, and the bark is soft against my feathers. I roost in the hollow by day, and at night I fly out to hunt. The hollow is safe, and the wood is strong. I can hear the stream from there, and the calls of the other owls. I am H

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It's deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit there at dusk, watching the meadow. The stream is a good place to drink, and the wood is safe from the dogs. I have a mate nearby, and we share the hollow. It's where I raise my young. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with branches that curl into the hollow. I roost in the middle, where the air is still and the wind does not touch me. The stream calls at night, and I answer. I have been here since the leaves fell, and I will stay until the snow comes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, with a high entrance. I sit there at dusk, watching the meadow, the lane, the stream. The stream is the best place for voles. I call to my mate there, and she answers. The hollow is where I roost, and where I nest with my young. It is safe, and it is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak at the edge of the wood. It's deep and dry, with a high entrance so the wind can't get in. I have a nest of dry leaves and down. I sit there all night, waiting for the road to be still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The oak is wide and deep, and the hollow is just big enough for me and my mate. We nest in the hollow, and I roost there too when the weather is bad.
